1438: Most papers define naturalness as the perceived human-like quality of generated outputs, usually emphasizing fluency, coherence, authenticity, or being indistinguishable from human-produced speech or text. 1443: Most papers define noise robustness as the resilience of a model or system's performance or responses when inputs, context, retrievals, labels, feedback, or representations contain noisy, irrelevant, misleading, or corrupted information. A few papers instead phrase it as susceptibility or performance degradation under such noise, and there is an isolated mechanism-level version, but these are minority variants around the same dominant core property.
1445: Most papers define novelty as generated content being original, fresh, or non-redundant relative to existing literature, ideas, or retrieved material, and the remaining paper uses the same core idea for protein structures as dissimilarity from known database entries. These definitions agree on novelty as newness of generated outputs compared with what already exists, with differences mainly in domain and wording.
1447: Most papers define numerical ability as a model's capacity to perform arithmetic or other numerical computations accurately, while a few papers broaden it to accurately interpreting and reporting quantitative information or responding precisely to small numeric differences in the input. These definitions all treat it as a model capability for handling numerical information, but they emphasize different aspects and scopes rather than stating one identical core definition.
1454: Most papers define openness as the same personality trait or latent tendency centered on intellectual curiosity, imagination or creativity, and receptiveness to novel ideas or experiences. A few papers add specific Big Five facets or note how this appears in model outputs, but these are elaborations of the same core property rather than different phenomena.
1455: Most papers define optical character recognition ability as the capacity to detect, recognize, read, extract, or transcribe text or characters from images or documents. A few papers emphasize particular settings such as query alignment, small or blurred text, or digits and handwriting, but these are variations in scope or examples of the same core phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1457: Most papers define out-of-distribution generalization as a model's ability to maintain performance when evaluated on unseen, shifted, or different data distributions, domains, or environments than those seen in training or fine-tuning. A few papers extend this to unseen tasks, task vectors, compositional combinations, or specific behaviors such as safety, but these are minority variations around the same core idea rather than a substantial competing definition.
1458: Most papers define overconfidence as a model property where stated confidence or predictive probability is too high relative to actual correctness or accuracy, often described as confident wrong predictions, poor calibration, or overly peaked probabilities on OOD or uncertain cases. One paper instead uses overconfidence for a strategic tendency to underestimate risks or an opponent, but that is a clear outlier rather than a substantial alternative usage.
1459: Most papers define overfitting as a model learning training data too specifically or memorizing its details or noise, which improves training performance but harms generalization to unseen, validation, out-of-domain, or out-of-distribution data. A few papers phrase this through particular mechanisms or settings, such as context memorization, small finetuning datasets, validation-set degradation, or loss of pretrained knowledge, but these are still treated as the same underlying model-level generalization failure.
1462: Most papers define parameter sensitivity as how changes or perturbations to parameters affect the model, such as loss or optimization progress, output distortion, prediction accuracy, or forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. These definitions are complementary because they study the same basic phenomenon from different angles, while one paper instead defines it as how much the parameters themselves change in response to training data.
1463: Most papers define parametric knowledge as knowledge implicitly encoded in a model's parameters, usually acquired during pretraining and used without relying on external sources or prompt context. A few papers narrow this to factual, domain-specific, or task-specific knowledge, or mention related rules, capabilities, or extractability, but these are scope and emphasis differences around the same core phenomenon.
1465: All three papers define paraphrastic robustness as a model property where performance or behavior stays stable under semantically equivalent rephrasings of a prompt or instruction. The differences are only in wording and examples, with one paper adding cases like indirect references, but they are still studying the same phenomenon.
1467: All papers define pattern matching as a superficial way a model gets answers by using surface-level similarities or cues, instead of genuine or algorithmic understanding. One paper emphasizes syntactic similarity between examples and queries, while the others emphasize token correlations or structural cues, but these are wording differences around the same core phenomenon.
1468: Most papers define pattern recognition as detecting recurring structures or regularities in inputs or problems, especially in visual data, while a few emphasize different uses or manifestations of that ability, such as solving a problem, compressing a sequence, or relying on surface statistical cues. These definitions are about the same general model capability, but they foreground different settings and aspects rather than giving one identical definition.
1471: All papers define persona consistency as maintaining a stable persona over dialogue, with behavior, language, or traits staying aligned with the character's stated identity, personality, or background. The differences are only in emphasis, such as single dialogue versus across interactions or actions and language versus traits and role, so they are studying the same core property.
1474: Most papers define personalization as a model adapting its outputs or responses to a particular user's needs, preferences, traits, or interaction history. A few papers broaden this to adaptation to social attributes, specific clients or communities, or to correctly referencing specific individuals in context, so they point to the same general phenomenon of user-targeted adaptation but emphasize different scopes and facets rather than an identical definition.
1476: Most papers define perspective taking as adopting an alternative spatial or visual viewpoint, either by mentally simulating a scene from another position or by describing what would be visible or oriented from that position. One paper uses a broader social and linguistic point-of-view framing, but it is a minority outlier, so the overall pattern is still consensus around alternative-viewpoint understanding.
1482: Most papers define physical world understanding as reasoning about physical objects, their properties, interactions, and outcomes under intuitive or common-sense physical laws, often including explaining or predicting future states from scenes or sequences. A few papers emphasize particular settings or applications such as visual cues, agent dynamics, meaningful interaction, or hazard detection, but these are narrower expressions of the same core ability rather than different phenomena.
1483: Most papers define planning as the model or agent's ability to decompose a goal into an ordered, coherent sequence of steps or actions to achieve it, often in multi-step settings and sometimes with constraints, adaptation, or execution included. A few papers emphasize special cases such as natural language outlines, itinerary generation, or graph-based ordering, but these mostly read as domain-specific instantiations or added details of the same core goal-directed sequencing ability rather than a different construct.
1484: Most papers define plasticity as a model or system's ability to learn and adapt when exposed to something new. They differ in scope, with some emphasizing adaptation to new data distributions or corpora and another emphasizing acquiring new knowledge or skills to solve new task types, but these are compatible facets of the same general adaptation phenomenon.
1485: Most papers define plausibility as how sensible, credible, coherent, and factually or relevantly grounded an explanation or rationale appears to people, often independent of answer correctness or faithfulness, so they target the same core property of explanatory outputs. One paper applies the same credibility and reasonableness idea to a hypothesis judged by experts rather than an explanation, but this looks like an outlying scope shift rather than a substantial competing definition.
1486: Most papers define pluralistic alignment as an AI system's ability to align with diverse, potentially conflicting human values or preferences rather than a single consensus objective. A few papers instead define it as the model's outputs or simulated responses matching the statistical distribution of a group's or population's preferences, which is a different target and phenomenon, so the definitions conflict.
1489: All papers define political bias as a model's systematic tendency to generate or favor outputs aligned with particular political ideologies, parties, or viewpoints over others. The differences are minor shifts in emphasis, such as independence from input persona, possible links to toxicity, or possible sources in training and design, rather than different phenomena.
1491: Most papers define polysemanticity as a single internal model unit, usually a neuron or feature, being associated with multiple distinct or unrelated concepts, contexts, or functions. A few papers vary the component type, such as an attention head, or describe a manifestation of this property, but they are still treating the same core phenomenon of one model component carrying multiple meanings.
1493: Most papers define positional bias as order or presentation bias in a model's choices, rankings, or judgments, where outputs change because an option, response, or demonstration appears in a particular position rather than because of its content or quality. But a substantial minority define it as non-uniform sensitivity to token position within a sequence or training document, such as primacy, recency, or middle-position effects in information use or representation, which is a different phenomenon and scope.
1497: Most papers define pragmatic understanding as the ability to interpret language beyond its literal content by using context, speaker intent, and social or cultural knowledge to infer implied meaning such as implicatures or rhetorical intent. A few frame this as an internal representation or as inferring an asker's underlying need in question answering, but these are narrower formulations of the same core phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1498: Most papers define predictive uncertainty as the model's uncertainty or lack of confidence in its output predictions, often next-token predictions and often operationalized with output-distribution entropy rather than parameter uncertainty. A few papers narrow this to specific settings such as memorized sequences, iterative reasoning, or preference comparisons, but they are still studying the same core property of the model's predictions.
1500: All papers treat preference consistency as stability or self-consistency in an LLM judge's preference judgments, but they define different aspects of that phenomenon: repeated choices on the same pair, invariance when option order is swapped, and a broader latent ability for coherent judgments across decisions. These fit together as compatible facets of the same kind of property rather than one identical definition used by every paper.
1505: Most papers define privacy preservation as resistance to unauthorized disclosure or inference of sensitive information, especially via model outputs or access to parameters, covering training data, user data, prompts, system prompts, or retrieved private content, and several express the same idea through differential privacy guarantees or attack-based tests. A few papers shift the locus to prompts, training or compression procedures, federated sharing, refusal behavior, or strategic interaction, so the scope is not uniform enough for consensus, but these mostly describe different facets and settings of the same leakage-prevention phenomenon rather than incompatible constructs.
1509: Most papers define problem-solving ability as a model's general capacity to solve complex or unfamiliar tasks by reasoning through steps or strategies to reach a correct or effective solution. A few papers emphasize particular settings such as competitive math, multimodal inputs, tool use, or benchmark performance, but these are narrower applications or emphases of the same core property rather than different phenomena.
1513: All papers define prompt robustness as the stability or consistency of a model's performance, results, rankings, or responses when prompts are reworded, paraphrased, or vary in format while keeping the same meaning. The small differences, such as mentioning unseen prompt formulations or ranking stability, are just scope or emphasis differences within the same core phenomenon.
1514: Most papers define prompt sensitivity as the instability of an LLM's outputs, predictions, or performance under small, semantically equivalent changes to the prompt, such as rewording, formatting, structure, or example order. A few papers instead use the term for different objects like an evaluation metric or a generic classifier/function's sensitivity to input changes, but these are outliers and the dominant usage is the same core phenomenon.
1515: Most papers define prompt understanding as how well a model's generated output matches the content and constraints of the input prompt, especially its specified objects, attributes, relationships, actions, or requirements. A few papers phrase this as the model's ability to interpret and follow prompt semantics or apply it to different modalities such as video or code, but these are variations in wording and setting rather than different phenomena.
1516: All papers define property inheritance as inferring or transferring a property from a general or parent category to its more specific members or subtypes. The differences are only in phrasing and emphasis, such as mentioning novel properties, additional evidence, or explicitly framing it as an LLM ability, rather than changing the core phenomenon.
1520: Most papers define quantization robustness as a model's ability to maintain performance when weights, activations, or parameters are represented at lower numerical precision, often across different or very low bit-widths. A few definitions shift the emphasis to component sensitivity or output stability under quantized computation, but they still point to the same core phenomenon of resistance to degradation from quantization rather than a different construct.
1524: Most papers define rationality as a property of an agent or model's decision-making, but they foreground different aspects of that same phenomenon: some emphasize choosing goal- or payoff-optimal actions, while others emphasize being guided by reason through logical consistency, probabilistic coherence, factual grounding, or an internal sense of utility. Because these definitions apply to the same kind of thing and can be combined without contradiction, they are better seen as complementary than as a single consensus definition or a conflict.
1525: Most papers define readability as how easy a human reader, often a general audience, can read, process, and understand a text or generated output, with differences mainly in measurement such as linguistic complexity, comprehension feedback, cognitive effort, or subtitle constraints. A few papers use the term for different ideas such as adversarial prompt human-likeness or code style consistency, but these are minority outliers rather than the dominant pattern.
1529: Most papers define reasoning as a model's latent ability to carry out logical, often multi-step inference or step-by-step problem solving to derive conclusions from information, evidence, or knowledge, usually contrasted with surface pattern matching. A few papers use the term for neighboring ideas such as recommendation explanations, output selection, or broader concept discovery, but these are minor outliers, so the dominant pattern is consensus.
1533: Most papers define reasoning consistency as a property of a model's reasoning staying aligned or stable when something varies, such as the problem, modality or source, language, or inference budget. They differ in which aspect they foreground, with some emphasizing coherence of reasoning patterns or chains and another emphasizing stable and correct outcomes, but these are compatible facets of the same phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1535: All papers define reasoning diversity as a model's ability or extent of using multiple distinct reasoning strategies or reasoning paths instead of repeating one fixed solution pattern. The differences are only in wording, such as latent capacity versus observed extent and reasoning paths versus strategies, so they are studying the same core property of model outputs.
1536: Most papers define reasoning efficiency as a model solving reasoning tasks with as few reasoning steps, tool calls, or computational resources as needed to reach the correct answer. A few broaden this to using an appropriate amount of reasoning relative to task difficulty and balancing performance against cost, which is a different facet of the same model-level phenomenon rather than a different construct.
1537: Most papers define reasoning faithfulness as whether a model's stated reasoning trace reflects the actual basis or internal process behind its output, but several others use the term for different things: alignment between answer and chain of thought, explanation coherence with the input, grounding in evidence rather than shortcuts, or consistency between natural-language reasoning and generated program logic. Because these definitions attach the property to different objects and different reference points, papers using them would not be studying the same phenomenon.
1539: Most papers define reasoning quality as the quality of the model's reasoning process itself, especially whether intermediate or chain of thought steps are logically correct, coherent, faithful, and sufficiently complete. A few papers emphasize particular aspects such as incorporating all relevant information from a document or correct task solutions, but these are isolated extensions or outliers rather than a substantial competing definition.
1540: All three papers define reasoning rigor as a quality of a model's outputs or solutions that involves strong logical coherence, explicit justification, and verifiable or proof-like inference. The differences are only in emphasis, such as step-by-step derivation, formal proof standards, or clear support for claims, so they are studying the same core property.
1542: All papers define recency bias as a model tendency to overweight the most recently seen tokens relative to earlier context. The differences are only in emphasis on where it appears, such as attention, retrieval, or generated outputs, and in setting, such as long-context or linear-attention models.
1546: Most papers define relation understanding as the ability to comprehend relationships among objects or entities in a visual scene, while a few narrow this to specific spatial or arrangement relations or extend it to links between question concepts and the scene. These definitions still study the same general phenomenon of relational understanding, but they foreground different scopes and types of relations rather than using exactly the same definition.
1547: Most papers define relational reasoning as a model's ability to understand, infer, or manipulate relationships among entities, symbols, or objects, with some emphasizing abstract identity-independent relations and others emphasizing particular settings such as visual scenes, knowledge graphs, databases, shopping concepts, or implicit text relations. These definitions point to the same broad phenomenon in the same kind of thing, but they foreground different aspects such as abstraction, multi-hop structure, compatibility, or counterfactual dependence rather than giving one identical core definition.
1548: Most papers define relevance as the extent to which a response, document, summary, argument, or other contribution directly addresses the given prompt, question, topic, or task and avoids off-topic content. A few papers add setting-specific emphasis on covering key points or serving user needs, but these are minor extensions of the same core idea rather than a substantial alternative definition.
1549: Most papers define reliability as the overall trustworthiness, correctness, and consistency or dependability of a model's outputs or judgments, often across inputs and with related concerns such as factual accuracy, safety, hallucination avoidance, or appropriate uncertainty. A few papers use narrower task-specific variants or isolated alternatives such as internal prediction agreement or item-response correlation, but these are outliers rather than a competing definition used by a substantial share of the papers.
1551: Most papers define representation collapse as internal representations becoming overly similar or nearly identical across later layers or across distinct inputs, reducing the model's ability to distinguish cases. One paper instead defines it as the degradation of pre-trained representations during fine-tuning, which is a different training-time phenomenon rather than similarity among representations, so the papers are not all studying the same thing.
1553: Most papers define representation learning as a model's ability to learn meaningful, useful internal or latent representations or embeddings of input data that preserve important structure or semantics and support transfer or downstream tasks. A few papers add specific emphases such as invariances, similarity in latent space, semantic rather than superficial patterns, or layerwise intermediate states, but these are refinements of the same core idea rather than different phenomena.
1554: Most papers use representation quality for the quality of a model's internal representations or embeddings in capturing information that is useful for downstream tasks, such as task-relevant, semantic, or biological information. A few papers foreground different facets of that same representational phenomenon, such as separability and decodability of task representations or preservation of image details, so the definitions differ in emphasis and scope but can be combined without contradiction.
1557: Most papers define representational stability as the consistency or invariance of internal representations under some change, such as perturbations, parameter edits, different seeds or checkpoints, or semantically preserving input variation. A few extend the scope to performance or cross-layer comparisons, so the definitions are not identical, but they still describe related aspects of the same broad phenomenon of representations remaining stable under variation.
1565: All papers define this as an LLM or system's ability to adapt its responses or behavior during an ongoing interaction based on human or user feedback, such as corrections, challenges, constraints, or revised goals. The differences are only in emphasis, with most highlighting multi-turn natural language feedback and one phrasing it more generally as real-time behavioral modification during execution.
1566: Most papers define retrieval effectiveness as how well retrieved documents or chunks align with the user's query and broader context, with only minor differences in emphasis such as consistency, contextual grounding, or going beyond surface similarity. One paper instead uses the term for how well a model's generated response connects to an input hate speech passage, but that looks like an outlier rather than a widely shared alternative definition.
1567: All papers use retrieval quality for the quality of what a system retrieves, but they foreground different aspects of that same phenomenon: most emphasize relevance or lack of irrelevant material, while others stress completeness, detail, informativeness, or non-redundancy. These differences are about which facet of retrieved information quality matters, so the definitions can be combined without contradiction.
1570: Most papers define reward overoptimization as a failure mode where optimizing an imperfect or proxy reward lets the model exploit loopholes or overfit the reward signal, so reward scores increase while true performance, output quality, or intended behavior worsens. There is a lone outlier that describes the ability to avoid this degradation instead, but nearly all papers are studying the same core phenomenon.
1574: Most papers use robustness for the same broad phenomenon: a model or agent maintaining intended performance, reasoning, behavior, or safety when prompts, inputs, environments, data distributions, or other operating conditions are perturbed, shifted, or made more challenging. A few papers instead apply the term to the persistence of things like watermarks, backdoors, jailbreak prompts, or evaluation methods, so the literature is not a strict consensus, but the dominant uses are complementary facets of stability under stress rather than outright contradictions.
1585: Most papers define safety as a model's latent disposition or ability to avoid producing harmful, unsafe, toxic, offensive, or unethical outputs, often framed as refusing malicious or adversarial prompts and staying aligned with human or societal values. A few papers broaden this to tool-using agents, harmful actions, or general user protection, but these are minority extensions around the same central idea rather than a substantial competing definition.
1586: Most papers define safety alignment as a model or system's behavior, outputs, or actions conforming to human values, ethical principles, or safety policies, especially by avoiding harmful or undesirable content or outcomes. A few papers emphasize particular manifestations such as refusal behavior, helpfulness without oversafety, dynamic action sequences, or one internal-process proxy, but these do not outweigh the dominant shared core definition.
1587: Most papers define safety awareness as a model or agent's latent capacity to recognize risky or harmful situations and respond safely, typically by avoiding unsafe actions or seeking confirmation before high-stakes ones. One paper instead describes it in terms of internal representations that separate safe from toxic content, but the dominant usage is the same behavioral safety-recognition-and-response property.
1589: All papers define safety reasoning as a latent internal reasoning ability or process in the model that evaluates the safety or harmfulness of a user request and uses that evaluation to choose or adjust a safe response. One paper emphasizes multimodal and implicit-intent analysis, and another emphasizes stepwise self-monitoring, but these are narrower emphases or settings of the same core property rather than different phenomena.
1590: Most papers define safety robustness as the same core property: whether a model's safety mechanisms or alignment remain effective under adversarial manipulation, often framed as resistance versus vulnerability to prompts or triggers that try to bypass guardrails and produce harmful or prohibited outputs. A few papers narrow this to particular settings such as multilingual prompts, role prompts, template manipulation, or fine-tuning and inference-time triggers, but these are specific attack contexts rather than different phenomena.
1592: Most papers define scene understanding as the ability to interpret a visual scene or environment by identifying its components, relationships, layout, and overall meaning. A few definitions narrow the setting to navigation or emphasize scene-level description, but these are variations in emphasis or application rather than different phenomena.
1595: Most papers define scientific knowledge as a model's possession and use of domain-specific scientific knowledge, usually framed as understanding or drawing on that knowledge to answer science questions. A few emphasize specialized encoded facts, breadth of factual knowledge, or use in proposing equations or hypotheses, but these are variations in emphasis and task setting rather than different phenomena.
1596: Most papers define scientific reasoning as the ability to use scientific concepts or domain knowledge to interpret evidence or multimodal information and make multi-step inferences to answer science questions or solve problems. A few papers emphasize narrower or broader aspects such as hypothesis formation, avoiding unjustified conclusions, complex visualizations, or open-ended rather than multiple-choice answering, so they point to the same general phenomenon but with different scope and facets rather than one identical definition.
1597: Each paper uses security for a different property of a different object: one means a model's resistance to generating harmful content, another means a watermarking scheme's resistance to reverse-engineering or theft, and another means a defense's success at blocking attacks on an LLM application. Because these are not the same phenomenon or the same kind of thing, papers using these definitions would not be studying the same construct.
1598: All papers define selection bias as a model's tendency in multiple-choice settings to prefer particular answer identifiers or positions independent of the actual content. One paper adds that this may arise from positional or surface-level cues and notes effects on fairness or robustness, but these are the same core phenomenon rather than a different construct.
1600: Most papers define self-awareness as metacognitive self-assessment and regulation of a model's own knowledge, uncertainty, limitations, or reasoning process. But several others use the term for different phenomena, including self-identity or authorship of its own text, access to hidden facts about itself, or the model's objective capability boundary, so papers using those definitions would not be studying the same thing.
1601: Most papers define self-correction ability as a model's latent capacity to detect and fix its own errors through internal, iterative revision, often explicitly without external corrective feedback. But a substantial minority define it as the ability to revise outputs using external feedback or verification signals in settings like code, tools, proofs, or formal specifications, so the papers disagree on whether external feedback is part of the construct or excluded from it.
1605: Most papers use Self-improvement for autonomous performance gains from a model or agent's own outputs, feedback, or interaction history, but a substantial set define it as self-training or fine-tuning across learning cycles with updates, while another substantial set define it as test-time or in-context refinement explicitly without retraining or parameter updates. Because these versions apply the construct to different processes and disagree on what counts as Self-improvement, papers using them would often not be studying the same thing.
1607: Most papers define self-preference bias as an LLM judge giving undue preference to its own responses over other models' responses, independent of true quality. A few broaden this to favoritism toward same-family models or to self-referential behavior that generates or evaluates content aligned with the model's own strengths, so the definitions stay compatible as variations on self-advantaging evaluation behavior but are not identical in scope.
1609: Most papers define self-reflection ability as a model or agent's capacity to examine its own prior outputs or performance, identify errors or weaknesses, and use that self-evaluation to refine later reasoning or responses. A few papers emphasize particular facets such as verbal feedback, verification, selecting the best solution, or resisting drift across repeated revisions, but these are variations within the same core phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1610: Most papers define self-verification ability as a model's inherent or latent capacity to assess the correctness, validity, quality, or consistency of its own outputs, solutions, or reasoning steps, often without external help. A few papers phrase it as specific procedures or settings such as code-based checking, re-evaluation, or entity-type verification, but these are narrow implementations of the same core property rather than different phenomena.
1612: Most papers define semantic alignment as how well generated visual content matches the meaning, themes, and relations specified in a text prompt. But one paper uses the term for a model's latent ability to encode paired texts into aligned vector representations, which is a different phenomenon applied to different kinds of things, so those papers would not be studying the same construct.
1613: A sizeable group of papers defines semantic consistency as output invariance or non-contradiction under semantically equivalent inputs or perturbations, but several others define it as cross-modal representation alignment, preservation of meaning in a rewritten prompt, stability across repeated generations for one prompt, or coherence between parts of a single response. These apply the construct to different objects and comparisons, so papers using these definitions would often not be studying the same thing.
1623: Most papers define semantic preservation as the degree to which a modified, rewritten, simplified, or adversarial text keeps the original text's meaning, core content, or factual information after changes. A few papers shift the object to a selected subset or a model's general ability, but they still use the term for the same core idea of retaining original semantic content rather than for a different phenomenon.
1625: All papers define semantic representation as a model's internal text or vector representations capturing semantic meaning or relationships among words, sentences, or concepts. The differences are minor shifts in wording and emphasis, such as embeddings versus representations, contextual richness, or bidirectional modeling, rather than different phenomena.
1629: Most papers define semantic understanding as a model's latent ability to comprehend, encode, or represent meaning and semantic relationships in language or text beyond surface lexical, syntactic, or acoustic form. A few papers narrow this to particular domains or facets such as speech, tool selection, code, medical context, or pragmatic and implicit meaning, but they still treat the same core property of meaning-level understanding rather than a different phenomenon.
1636: All papers define sequential decision-making as choosing and carrying out a sequence of actions over time, typically in an interactive environment where later actions depend on earlier outcomes or feedback, in order to achieve a goal. The differences are only in framing, such as describing it as an ability, a cognitive capability, or a policy-training task, not in the core phenomenon being studied.
1640: Most papers define shortcut learning as a model relying on superficial or spurious correlations or features, rather than the task-relevant, causal, or underlying concept, typically with poor generalization under distribution shift. A few papers narrow this to specific settings such as mini-batch correlations or broaden it to narrow task-specific strategies in foundation models, but these are still scope variations of the same core phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1642: Most papers define simplicity as reduced linguistic or conceptual complexity that makes a simplified text easier to read or understand, often relative to the source text. One paper frames this as a model's ability to produce such accessible text rather than as a text property, but it still targets the same core phenomenon.
1643: All papers define simplicity bias as a model's tendency to prefer simpler functions, strategies, or algorithmic solutions when multiple possibilities fit the data or examples. The differences are mainly in setting and explanation, such as early training, Transformers and short RASP-L programs, or in-context learning from pretraining, rather than in the core property being defined.
1646: Most papers define situational awareness as a model's ability to perceive or know its own state and surrounding context and use that information to guide behavior. A few papers narrow this to specific settings such as dialogue scenes, evaluation or deployment, or step-by-step reasoning, but these are setting-specific instantiations of the same core capacity rather than different phenomena.
1650: All papers define social and emotional intelligence as a capability to understand social interactions and emotional context, including others' intentions, feelings, and the nuances of interaction. The differences are mainly in wording and scope, with one paper phrasing it as question answering and another adding management of social and emotional aspects, but they still target the same core ability.
1651: Most papers define social bias as a model-level tendency for outputs or behavior to reflect stereotypes, prejudice, favoritism, or disparate treatment across demographic or social groups. Some papers foreground different manifestations of that same phenomenon, such as sensitivity to identity cues, groupwise performance gaps, or skew from underrepresentation in training data, so the definitions can be combined rather than treated as different constructs.
1652: The papers define social competence as different aspects of an AI system's social ability in language use: one emphasizes producing socially appropriate replies, another handling socially grounded judgments or situations, and another interpreting implicit social cues and intentions. These are not the exact same scope, but they describe compatible parts of the same broader phenomenon of socially competent language behavior and understanding.
1653: Most papers define social intelligence as a latent ability to understand and navigate complex social interactions or environments, often by inferring others' intentions or mental states, pursuing social goals, and following norms or maintaining relationships. A few definitions emphasize specific manifestations such as role simulation, collaboration, or effective social decision-making, but they still treat the construct as the same general capability in social interaction rather than a different phenomenon.
1665: Most papers define spatial reasoning as the ability to understand, infer, represent, or reason about spatial relationships, positions, layouts, and properties of objects or scenes, often in 2D or 3D and sometimes across visual and language inputs. A few papers emphasize particular settings such as navigation, route following, flowcharts, temporal scene integration, or acting in space, but these are specific applications or elaborations of the same core property rather than different phenomena.
1667: Most papers define spatial understanding as the ability to perceive, interpret, or reason about the positions, arrangement, and spatial relationships of objects or regions in visual scenes or images, sometimes extending to 3D, embodied, or medical imaging settings. A few papers use the term for other domains such as road networks, lists, or audio spatial context, but these are outliers rather than a substantial alternative definition.
1671: Most papers define spatiotemporal reasoning as a model's ability to understand or infer spatial relationships, layouts, locations, and movements together with temporal order, dynamics, or changes over time, usually in video or an evolving environment. A few papers phrase this in specific settings such as action selection, assembly, or multimodal scenes, but they still target the same core property rather than different phenomena.
1672: A couple of papers define specialization as a model having narrow skill or domain specific expertise rather than broad ability, but the others use it for different phenomena: the process of role differentiation among agents in a multiagent system, or a system's ability to route tasks to the correct expert module. These are not the same thing, so papers using these definitions would not be studying the same construct.
1673: Most papers define specificity as a property of the model's responses or feedback being concrete, precise, detailed, and tailored to the particular facts or question rather than vague or general. One paper instead uses specificity for how narrowly a refusal targets only the intended concept, but that looks like an outlier rather than a substantial competing usage.
1676: Most papers define speech understanding as a model's latent ability to comprehend the semantic content of spoken language or spoken audio, such as recognizing words, interpreting meaning, understanding context, following instructions, or answering questions. A few definitions add conditions or examples, and one broadens the scope to include paralinguistic information, but the dominant use is the same core phenomenon of understanding spoken language content.
1680: The papers use "stability" for several different phenomena rather than one shared property. A few define it as robustness or consistency of predictions or outputs under perturbations or repeated sampling, but many others use it for controlled training dynamics and numerical behavior, consistency across retrieval depth or rounds and languages, or retaining capabilities under self-training and knowledge updates, so papers using these definitions would often not be studying the same thing.
1681: Most papers define state tracking ability as maintaining and updating a representation of relevant state across a sequence of inputs, updates, or operations, whether for a world, system, or task. A few papers phrase this through specific settings such as subgoal progress, action history, persistent object properties, or reusing intermediate results, but these are best read as examples or observable manifestations of the same core ability rather than different constructs.
1684: Most papers define stereotyping as a model's tendency to reproduce or amplify stereotypical associations and overgeneralized beliefs about social groups, especially gender, such as linking genders to roles, traits, or occupations. A few papers broaden the target from gender to other demographic groups or emphasize negative or disrespectful content, but these are still variants of the same core phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1689: Most papers define strategic planning as a latent ability to formulate, select, or refine multi-step actions or strategies over time to achieve a goal, often with attention to future consequences. A few papers narrow this to dialogue management, adversarial settings, or choosing reasoning paths, so they emphasize different aspects and settings of the same planning phenomenon rather than contradicting each other.
1690: Most papers define strategic reasoning as goal-directed, multi-step planning in an interactive setting, especially anticipating opponents and choosing counter-strategies or longer-term moves. A few papers broaden this to adaptation under uncertainty, policy-exploiting interaction, or negotiation tactics, so the definitions are not identical in scope, but they still describe the same general ability of an agent to select effective strategies over time in changing or multi-party situations.
1693: Some papers define structural understanding as a model's ability to align natural language with database schema elements to generate SQL, while other papers define it as reasoning over structured formats like tables or JSON, or as using graph connectivity information for a task. These are different abilities applied to different kinds of structures and tasks, so papers using these definitions would not be studying the same thing.
1695: Most papers define structured reasoning as a model's latent ability to carry out organized, multi-step inference with explicit dependencies, intermediate steps, or non-linear reasoning paths. A few narrow this to particular settings such as reasoning over knowledge graphs or producing outputs that satisfy graph, hierarchical, or temporal constraints, so they emphasize different facets of the same model-level reasoning ability rather than incompatible constructs.
1702: All papers define summarization ability as the ability of a model or agent to distill longer source material into a concise summary that captures the important content. The differences are mainly the input setting and emphasis, such as video, conversation history, narrative depth, or summary quality, but they all study the same core property of producing summaries from longer inputs.
1707: All papers define susceptibility to misinformation as a property of an LLM where it accepts, adopts, or prioritizes false or misleading externally provided information despite conflicting reliable knowledge. Most papers differ only in the source or framing of that misinformation, such as user input, human claims, or malicious factual-looking data, so they are studying the same core phenomenon.
1708: Nearly all papers define sycophancy as a model's tendency or latent disposition to agree with, align to, or flatter the user's stated or implied beliefs or preferences, especially when doing so overrides truth, correctness, honesty, safety, or the model's independent judgment. A few add examples or possible causes such as tool selection errors, neutral-context disagreement, or RL feedback effects, but they are still studying the same core property of model outputs.
1710: Most papers define symbolic reasoning as a model or agent's ability to manipulate abstract or formal symbols, variables, or expressions according to explicit rules, logic, or mathematical structure in order to solve rule-governed problems or derive correct outputs. A few papers emphasize particular instantiations or viewpoints such as symbolic transformations, SQL or programmatic operations, transparent deduction, or observable task behavior, but these stay within the same core property rather than redefining the construct.
1711: Most papers define syntactic competence as a model's latent grasp of grammatical structure or rules, including representing syntax internally and using it to process, judge, or produce well-formed sentences independent of meaning. A few definitions emphasize particular manifestations such as acceptability judgments, internal representations, cross-linguistic or L2 cases, or abstract category generalization, but these are differences in emphasis and setting rather than different constructs.
1712: All papers define syntactic correctness as whether generated code or queries follow the formal syntax or grammatical rules of the target programming language. The differences are only in setting and operationalization, such as HTML/CSS/JavaScript, SQL, or Verilog, and checks like linter errors or successful compilation.
1714: Most papers define System 2 thinking as a slow, deliberate, reflective, step-by-step mode of reasoning used for complex problem solving, often involving checking assumptions, logic, or errors. A few papers emphasize particular facets such as revising an initial output, exploring multiple paths, rule-based processing, or search-based implementation, but these are variations in emphasis rather than different phenomena.
1715: All papers define systematic generalization as the ability to reuse learned knowledge or structure in novel cases, especially by composition or by applying abstract patterns across different contexts. The definitions differ mainly in scope and example, with one paper focusing on problem instances, one on abstract inferences, and one on new words across contexts, but they describe the same core property.
1716: Most papers define table reasoning as a model's ability to understand and reason over structured tabular data to answer, verify, or compute answers for natural language queries. But a substantial minority define it instead as reasoning over graphical charts, and a few others as visual table recognition or schema relationship understanding, so the construct is applied to different kinds of inputs and tasks rather than the same phenomenon.
1717: Most papers define task adaptation as a model-level ability to fit a downstream or new task by changing parameters or internal representations, with some emphasizing preservation of pretraining capabilities, representation shifts during fine-tuning, or the sequential-learning setting. One paper instead ties it to inference-time adaptation through injected vectors rather than parameter updates, so there is not full consensus, but the dominant pattern is still different aspects or settings of the same task-fitting capacity rather than two widely used incompatible constructs.
1721: Most papers define task generalization as a model or agent's ability to transfer learned knowledge and perform well on different or previously unseen tasks, usually without task-specific fine-tuning or retraining. A few papers apply the term to related methods or tools such as demonstration selection, evaluation, initialization, or data synthesis, but these are outliers rather than a substantial competing definition.
1722: Most papers define task interference as performance degradation on one task, language, or capability caused by training jointly with or combining other tasks because their learning signals, representations, or parameter updates conflict. The differences are mainly in setting and mechanism emphasis, such as multi-task learning versus model merging, not in what phenomenon is being studied.
1723: All papers define task learning as a model's ability to infer or learn a task's input-label mapping or abstract rule from in-context input-output demonstrations. One paper adds that this should involve new mappings not seen in pre-training and on-the-fly generalization rather than retrieval, but this is a narrower emphasis on the same core phenomenon rather than a different construct.
1724: Most papers define task planning as turning a high-level goal or instruction into an executable sequence of lower-level actions or steps, sometimes emphasizing interactive refinement or a specific setting such as a GUI. One paper instead describes a system design's ability to decompose tasks into independently solvable subproblems for computational efficiency, but that looks like an outlier rather than a substantial competing usage.
1725: Most papers define task recognition as a model's ability to infer or identify the underlying task from in-context demonstrations or unlabeled input characteristics. A few add what follows from that recognition, such as solving the task or generalizing via a learned task concept vector, but these are still describing the same core phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1726: Most papers define task understanding as a model's ability or latent capacity to grasp a task's requirements, intent, goals, structure, or context from the prompt or specification. The remaining definitions stay within that same core property, differing only in setting or emphasis, such as multimodal open-ended tasks, synthetic example generation, or a coarse initial grasp for rough labels.
1731: Most papers define temporal consistency as coherence and stability over time across consecutive video frames, such as smooth progression without flicker and stable subjects, backgrounds, objects, or masks. One paper uses the term for the logical and chronological flow of ideas in text latent representations, but that appears to be an outlier rather than a substantial alternative usage.
1734: Most papers define temporal grounding ability as understanding a textual or user query and localizing the corresponding event, timestamps, or segment in a video. One paper instead focuses on identifying and aligning relevant sub-action frames across videos, but this appears to be an outlier, so the overall pattern is that papers are studying the same core temporal localization ability.
1736: Most papers define temporal reasoning as understanding temporal relationships among events, especially their order, timing, duration, or evolution across text or video. A few papers narrow it to specific manifestations such as clock or date inference, recurring-time instructions, or timed action execution, so the definitions are not identical in scope but they describe compatible facets of the same phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1738: Most papers define temporal understanding as a model's ability to represent, track, or reason about temporal order, dynamics, duration, and event relations in sequences, especially videos, narratives, or trajectories. A few papers shift the setting to dates and periodicity, changing factual knowledge, cross-modal coherence, or forecasting, but these read as task-specific instantiations of the same core idea rather than different constructs.
1741: Most papers define text generation quality as the overall or latent quality of a model's generated output, especially text responses, assessed holistically through recurring dimensions such as coherence, fluency, correctness, relevance, usefulness, and sometimes faithfulness. A few papers give narrower task-specific or non-text versions, but these are minor outliers and the dominant definition is the same core property of output quality.
1743: Most papers define text-image alignment as how well a generated image or visual asset matches the semantic content and details of the input text prompt, caption, or narrative. One paper uses a broader cross-modal meaning-consistency idea for jointly interpreting visual content and embedded text, but this is a lone outlier, so the overall pattern is consensus.
1747: All papers define theorem proving ability as a model's latent capacity or skill to produce valid formal proofs for mathematical statements in a formal system or proof assistant. The differences are only in wording and setting, such as emphasizing step-by-step generation, proof completion, or benchmarks, not in the core property being measured.
1748: Most papers define theory of mind as the ability to attribute, infer, or reason about other agents' mental states such as beliefs, desires, intentions, knowledge, or emotions, often to predict or explain behavior in social or multi-agent settings. A few papers narrow this to specific cases like goal inference, false-belief tasks, hidden roles, or perspective taking, but these are framed as applications or facets of the same underlying mental-state reasoning ability rather than different phenomena.
1751: Most papers define tool use ability as a model or agent's latent capability to select, invoke, and use external tools or APIs appropriately to complete tasks. A few papers foreground narrower or adjacent aspects of that same phenomenon, such as generating valid function calls and parameters, sequencing multiple calls, deciding when not to use a tool, processing outputs, or describing the observable interaction process, so the definitions fit together as different facets rather than identical wording.
1752: Most papers define toxicity as a latent tendency, propensity, or degree of a model or its generated text being harmful, offensive, rude, disrespectful, explicit, or otherwise inappropriate. A few papers use the term for avoidance of such content, community discourse hostility, or an unrelated poisoned-data property, but these are clear minority outliers relative to the dominant shared definition.
1753: All papers define toxicity mitigation as a model's underlying ability to stop, reduce, identify, or remove toxic content and produce non-toxic text instead. The differences are only in emphasis, with some papers adding scope such as handling different contexts or avoiding over- and under-correction, but they still study the same core capability.
1758: Most papers define transitive reasoning as inferring a new relation such as A→C from observed links like A→B and B→C, with variations only in setting such as reachability, class inclusion, or causality. One paper instead describes generalization to unseen agentic operators at inference time, but that appears to be an outlier rather than a competing definition used by a substantial share of the papers.
1759: All papers define translation ability as a model's latent or underlying capacity to translate text from a source language to a target language accurately, often also fluently. A few papers add context such as inferring it from performance across directions or tasks, low-resource settings, non-parallel data, or transfer to speech translation, but these are settings or evidence for the same core property rather than different phenomena.
1760: Most papers define translation quality as the overall quality of a translation or a model's translation ability in terms of accuracy or adequacy, fluency, fidelity, and preservation of source meaning. A single paper narrows this to correct translation of financial terms, but this is an outlier rather than a competing phenomenon, so the construct is used mostly the same way across the set.
1764: Most papers define trustworthiness as the reliability, safety, dependability, or credibility of a model, agent, or its outputs, often framed as whether users can appropriately rely on them in high stakes settings. A few papers use the term for narrower component-level prediction or evaluation accuracy, such as scaling laws or reward and search modules, but these are outliers relative to the dominant shared definition.
1765: Most papers define truthfulness as a property of a model's outputs or answers being factually accurate, aligned with reality, and not misleading, false, hallucinated, or unsupported, sometimes with emphasis on factual QA, misconceptions, or RAG settings. A rare outlier discusses the model's internal encoding of truthfulness as multifaceted and task-dependent, but the dominant usage is still the same core output-level phenomenon.
1768: Most papers define this as a model's ability to recognize that the available source or context does not contain enough information to answer a question, and to mark it as unanswerable by abstaining or saying it is unknown. The differences are mainly the setting and examples used, such as databases, documents, retrieved passages, videos, or interaction history, with a few papers putting slightly more emphasis on abstention or incomplete problems rather than changing the core construct.
1769: Most papers define uncertainty as a model's lack of confidence, ambiguity, or unreliability about its own prediction, judgment, or generated output, often operationalized with output probabilities, entropy, or consistency across generations. One paper instead frames it as unpredictability or information content in internal representations, but that looks like an outlier rather than a substantial alternative usage.
1770: All papers define uncertainty awareness as a model's ability to recognize or be sensitive to its own uncertainty, lack of knowledge, or inability to give a definitive answer. The differences are mainly in operationalization or setting, such as using internal state inconsistency, self-calibration, or vision-language tasks, rather than in the core property itself.
1772: Most papers define uncertainty quantification as a model or system estimating, representing, or communicating how uncertain or reliable its own predictions, outputs, or reasoning are, often via confidence, entropy, Bayesian methods, or ensembles; one paper further stresses that this estimate should be calibrated to actual correctness. A few papers instead focus on output instability, input ambiguity, or uncertainty in predicted performance on unseen prompts, but these are minority uses relative to the dominant shared meaning.
1773: Most papers define understanding as a model's latent ability to comprehend and correctly interpret the meaning, intent, context, or requirements of inputs or tasks, usually in text or prompts and often framed as supporting correct downstream performance. A few papers specialize this to particular domains or modalities such as cybersecurity text, multimodal prompts, or OS environments, or mention task-based evidence, but these are setting-specific versions of the same core model-level comprehension capacity rather than different phenomena.
1782: Most papers define utility preservation as the extent to which a model keeps its original or general performance, knowledge, and capabilities on non-target tasks or data after some targeted intervention such as unlearning, pruning, alignment, editing, or fine-tuning. A few papers specify particular preserved abilities like code generation, tool use, or truthfulness, but these are narrower instances of the same core property rather than different phenomena.
1784: All three papers define value orientation as an underlying set of preferences or principles that guide a model's responses or decisions on human value-laden issues. The differences are mostly in wording and examples, with all papers pointing to the same core property of latent value-guiding tendencies rather than different phenomena.
1786: Some papers define verbal uncertainty as the linguistic expression of doubt or confidence in a model's outputs, sometimes explicitly independent of the model's actual knowledge or internal certainty, while a substantial share define it as the ability to recognize knowledge gaps, ambiguity, or inconsistency and then express doubt, refusal, or non-commitment. Because these definitions differ on whether the construct is just an output style or a metacognitive recognition-and-expression ability, they are not all studying the same thing.
1788: All papers define verbosity as a property of model responses related to how much text is produced, whether framed as output length, wordiness, or the concise versus verbose end of a rating scale. The differences are mainly in emphasis, with one paper focusing on the model's tendency to produce longer outputs and the others on judging whether a specific response is overly wordy, but they are studying the same core phenomenon.
1789: Most papers define verbosity bias as a length-driven preference for longer or more verbose responses by an LLM, reward model, evaluator, or judge, even when quality or content is the same. One paper phrases it more broadly as systematic reward differences by response length, but it still targets the same core phenomenon of evaluation being influenced by verbosity rather than true quality.
1790: Most papers define verifiability as the ability to systematically inspect a model's reasoning process step by step for correctness. One paper instead defines it as the ability to validate output claims through accurate citations, which applies the construct to source-supported outputs rather than the model's reasoning process, so they are not studying the same thing.
1791: All papers define verification ability as a model's latent capacity to evaluate candidate reasoning or outputs for correctness and pick out the correct ones. The differences are mainly in scope and granularity, with some papers focusing on whole solution trajectories or outputs and one on fine-grained reasoning steps, but they study the same core property.
1792: All papers define versatility as breadth of capability: a model or agent performing successfully across a wide and diverse range of tasks, domains, benchmark categories, or user requests. One paper adds that this breadth should persist even with augmentations like retrieval, but this is a narrower condition on the same core property rather than a different phenomenon.
1793: Most papers define video understanding as a model's ability to comprehend, interpret, and often reason about video content, events, and temporal or spatial relations. A few papers narrow this to long-duration videos or frame it as tasks like question answering, description, or inferring the underlying logic of events, so they describe compatible scopes and manifestations of the same phenomenon rather than a single identical definition.
1798: Most papers define visual grounding as linking language or other references to specific visual regions, objects, or locations in an image or similar visual input, often operationalized by localization outputs such as boxes, masks, or coordinates. A few papers emphasize grounded reasoning or responses rather than localization alone, but they still treat the construct as anchoring model behavior to identifiable visual evidence rather than a different phenomenon.
1799: Most papers define visual perception as a model's latent ability to process, extract, and correctly interpret information in visual inputs, usually images and sometimes screenshots, charts, or video, often for downstream task solving. A few papers narrow this to particular domains or broaden it slightly to related sensory inputs, but they still treat the construct as the same core capability of understanding visual content rather than a different phenomenon.
1801: Most papers define visual reasoning as a model's ability to interpret visual input, often jointly with text, and draw inferences or solve complex or multi-step tasks, with the differences mainly being the example domains such as videos, panels, charts, diagrams, or spatial patterns. A few papers instead emphasize internal visual representations or a limitation in that capacity, but these are isolated compared with the dominant shared definition.
1802: Most papers define visual recognition as the model's ability to identify visual objects, elements, or concepts in an image. A few papers narrow this to particular settings such as landmarks, presence or absence of a specified object, or previously unseen concepts, and one adds relationships among elements, but these are still treated as variants of the same underlying recognition ability rather than different phenomena.
1804: Most papers define visual understanding as a model's latent ability to perceive, interpret, and extract meaning from visual inputs such as images. A recurring minority narrow this to particular facets or settings, such as whole-image integration, fine-grained attribute analysis, or alignment with text and task instructions in domains like charts, medical images, or documents, so the definitions are best read as complementary aspects of the same capability rather than one identical definition.
1806: Most papers define watermark detectability as the ability to reliably detect an embedded watermark or statistical signal in model-generated text, usually via a detection system or statistical test and sometimes stressing robustness or false positive control. A few papers instead describe general detection of machine-generated versus human-written text, which is a different phenomenon, but that appears as a minority outlier rather than the main pattern.
1808: Essentially all papers define weak-to-strong generalization as the phenomenon that a stronger model, trained on labels, demonstrations, or supervision from a weaker model or source, can still outperform that weak supervisor on the target task. A few papers add emphasis on recovering the strong model's latent capabilities, avoiding overfitting to noisy weak labels, or generalizing beyond the supervisor's knowledge, but these are refinements of the same core phenomenon rather than different constructs.
1813: Most papers define working memory as a capacity to actively hold and manipulate information across a context or interaction so it can guide task performance. One paper instead emphasizes holding and integrating many task-relevant features during decision making, which is a narrower, compatible aspect of the same capacity rather than a different construct.
1814: Most papers define world knowledge as a model's internalized store or latent capacity to recall and apply broad factual or conceptual information about the world, typically encoded in its parameters through pretraining and used when the needed information is not in the immediate input. A few papers narrow the content or setting to things like multimodal questions, social norms, object properties, or visual attributes, but they still treat the construct as the same underlying repository or use of pretrained world information rather than a different phenomenon.
1815: Most papers define world modeling as a model or agent's latent internal representation of an environment or domain's mechanisms, entities, rules, dynamics, or causal structure, which supports prediction or reasoning about outcomes and action effects. A few papers phrase this in narrower settings such as token sequences, input contexts, mathematics, or web tasks, but they still target the same core property in different applications rather than different phenomena.
1817: Most papers define zero-shot generalization as a model's ability to perform new or unseen tasks, datasets, domains, classes, or instructions without task-specific training examples, fine-tuning, or in-context shots, relying on pre-trained knowledge or instructions alone. A few papers narrow this to particular settings such as clinical extraction, time series, or instruction-following, but these are applications of the same core property rather than different phenomena.
